text: If two circles cut one another, (then) they will not have the same center. For let the two circles $ABC$ and $CDG$ cut one another at points $B$ and $C$. I say that they will not have the same center.
For, if possible, let $E$ be (the common center),

frame.supposition: point $E$ is the (common) center of the circles $ABC$ and $CDG$

text: and let $EFG$ be drawn through (the two circles), at random.
And since point $E$ is the center of the circle $ABC$, $EC$ is equal to $EF$.

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: point $E$ is the center of the circle $ABC$

text: Again, since point $E$ is the center of the circle $CDG$, $EC$ is equal to $EG$.

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: point $E$ is the center of the circle $CDG$

text: But $EC$ was also shown (to be) equal to $EF$.

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: $EC$ was also shown (to be) equal to $EF$

text: Thus, $EF$ is also equal to $EG$, the lesser to the greater.
assertion: EF is equal to EG (the lesser to the greater)

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: $EF$ is also equal to $EG$, the lesser to the greater

text: Thus, point $E$ is not the (common) center of the circles $ABC$ and $CDG$.
assertion: point E is not the common center of circles ABC and CDG

frame.closes: point $E$ is the (common) center of the circles $ABC$ and $CDG$

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: point $E$ is not the (common) center of the circles $ABC$ and $CDG$

text: Thus, if two circles cut one another, (then) they will not have the same center. (Which is) the very thing it was required to show.
